editorNote: A $4,000 household robot rolls into view while compatibles, hard disks, databases, and modems show where practical computing is heading.
morningLine: This week in 1984: Hubot promises a robotic companion for the living room, even if the chores remain yours.

lead.headline: The $4,000 Robot Rolls Into the Home
lead.dek: Hubot brings a smiling electronic companion, a serving tray, and a steep price into the consumer marketplace.
body: A mobile robot called Hubot went on sale this week for $4,000, offering households a distinctly 1984 vision of electronic companionship. The machine could move around the home, speak through a synthesized voice, and carry objects on a tray while presenting a friendly face on its display.

The sales pitch mixed science fiction with carefully limited reality. Hubot could entertain, communicate, and serve as a rolling presence, but it could not brew coffee, wash windows, or clean the floor. It could carry a cup once someone else had filled it.

That contrast captures the state of home robotics. Microprocessors, sensors, speech, and compact electronics make a personable machine possible, yet reliable household manipulation remains far harder than rolling across a room. Hubot is closer to an electronic companion and conversation piece than an automated servant.

Even so, the launch matters because it puts a consumer price and a retail proposition on the domestic robot. At $4,000, Hubot is costlier than many complete personal-computer systems, but it turns the robot from a laboratory spectacle into something a determined buyer can order.

stories.headline: Digital Equipment Pays $1.1 Million Export Fine
body: Digital Equipment Corp. was fined $1.1 million after computers reached the Soviet bloc through an unauthorized export route, according to a September 6 report. The penalty underscores how strategic Washington considers advanced computing equipment.

The case places computer makers in a difficult global market: demand is international, but export controls can follow machines far beyond the first sale. For one of the industry’s largest minicomputer companies, compliance has become as consequential as engineering.

stories.headline: September's PC Market Fills With Compatibles and Databases
body: September periodicals show the IBM-compatible market broadening quickly. Creative Computing examined the low-cost Sanyo 555 while devoting a special section to database-management choices for buyers trying to turn hardware into useful office systems.

Software competition is just as visible. Borland is advertising Turbo Pascal and Sidekick at prices intended to bring serious programming and desktop utility tools within reach of individual PC owners.

stories.headline: Hard Disks Promise to End Macintosh Floppy Shuffling
body: The Tecmar Mac Drive offers Macintosh owners fixed and removable storage beyond the machine’s built-in floppy drive. Configurations include 10 megabytes of fixed storage or 5 megabytes removable, with another removable option available.

For users juggling programs and documents across disks, a hard drive changes the rhythm of the Macintosh. The capacities remain modest by institutional standards, but desktop access to megabytes of online storage makes the graphical machine far more practical for sustained work.
